title: Sizing a bulk order: specification, capacity and materials

say: Sizing a bulk order: specification, capacity and materials.
This is the video for module 1 of Bulk Production Planning.
When an order is 50 or 100 times your usual size, five things change at once. First, materials you buy before you earn anything.

say: Most bulk enquiries arrive as a call or a WhatsApp voice note, like, we need about 5,000 packs of chips before Christmas, what is your price?
Turn that into a one-page order specification sheet that you and the buyer both agree.

panel.heading: The order specification sheet
items: Documents, one contact, changes in writing

say: Write the exact product and size, for example 100 g per pack, and the exact quantity.

panel.heading: The order specification sheet
items: Documents, one contact, changes in writing

say: Write the packaging, the labels, and the quality standard: the approved sample and what counts as a defect.

panel.heading: The order specification sheet
items: Documents, one contact, changes in writing

say: Write the delivery date, address and who receives.

panel.heading: The order specification sheet
items: Documents, one contact, changes in writing

say: Write the unit price, the deposit, and when the balance is paid.

panel.heading: The order specification sheet
items: Documents, one contact, changes in writing

say: Finally, the documents the buyer needs, one named person on each side, and the rule that any change is confirmed in writing.
Reply to the enquiry with questions, not a price. Serious buyers respect this.

panel.heading: The order specification sheet
items: Documents, one contact, changes in writing

say: For example, Kemi makes plantain chips in Ibadan. A normal weekend order is 40 packs. A company asks for 5,000 packs for staff hampers. That is 125 times her normal order.
She uses about 0.30 kg of raw plantain per pack, so 5,000 packs need 1,500 kg, before any waste.
Frying oil goes from 1 litre to 125 litres.
Her fryer makes about 80 packs an hour, so that is 62.5 hours of frying alone.
And 50 packs fill a carton, so she needs space for 100 cartons, clean, dry and off the floor.
So this is not a busy weekend. Kemi must plan days, not hours.

panel.heading: Kemi: from 40 packs to 5,000
panel.rule: Plan days, not hours. The bottleneck decides your finish date.

say: Never quote from your best-ever day. Time each step with your phone's stopwatch, three times, and use the average.
The slowest step is the bottleneck. For Kemi, frying at 80 packs an hour sets the pace for the whole line.

panel.heading: Three numbers replace guesswork
items: Bottleneck: the slowest step per hour
Sustained daily rate: average of 10 days
Takt time: available time / units needed

say: Next, average your good units over your last 10 full working days. Kemi's average is 470 packs a day, so 5,100 packs, including 2% extra, need 11 production days.

panel.heading: Three numbers replace guesswork
items: Bottleneck: the slowest step per hour
Sustained daily rate: average of 10 days
Takt time: available time / units needed

say: Takt time is the available time divided by the units needed. For Kemi, one pack must leave the sealer about every 0.9 minutes.

panel.heading: Three numbers replace guesswork
items: Bottleneck: the slowest step per hour
Sustained daily rate: average of 10 days
Takt time: available time / units needed

say: And count only units that pass your quality check. Counting rejects makes every later plan too optimistic.

panel.heading: Three numbers replace guesswork
items: Bottleneck: the slowest step per hour

say: Build a bill of materials from your own weighed batches, including packaging. Then add three allowances. Overrun is extra you make so samples and rejects do not leave you short.

cards.d: Extra units for samples and rejects. Kemi plans 2%, so 5,100 packs for 5,000.
Loss before a unit exists, like bruised plantain. Kemi adds 5% on plantain.
Pouches lost to bad seals or misprints. Kemi adds 3% on pouches and labels.

say: Material waste is loss before a unit exists. Kemi adds 5% on plantain, so she buys about 1,607 kg.

say: Packaging spoilage covers bad seals and misprints. Then round up to how suppliers sell. Kemi orders 11 packs of 500 pouches, which is 5,500.

say: Long-lead items like printed pouches, labels and cartons are ordered first, as soon as the deposit arrives and the artwork is approved. Printed pouches can take 10 working days.

panel.heading: What to buy first, what to buy in lots

say: Perishables must not all arrive on day one. Kemi buys plantain in four lots of about 400 kg, each the day before it is needed.
Check every delivery against your specification before you sign or pay.

panel.heading: What to buy first, what to buy in lots

say: Pushing the bottleneck harder is where accidents happen. Keep the oil pot no more than about one-third full, never leave it unattended, keep a fire blanket close, and never pour water on an oil fire.
Keep food materials off the floor and covered.
And never release goods until payment has actually landed in your account, not just a screenshot or SMS alert.

panel.heading: Safety and scam checks
items: Oil pot no more than one-third full
Fire blanket close; no water on oil fire
Food stock off the floor, covered

say: To remember. Write the specification sheet and keep a golden sample.
Plan with your sustained rate. Add allowances and round up. Order long-lead items first, perishables in lots.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Turn every enquiry into a specification sheet
Plan with your sustained rate, not your best day
Add allowances, round up to pack sizes
Order long-lead items first, perishables in lots
